headline: プラン is borrowed from English plan.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English plan.

headline: Katsu has a Heian accent that implies it is the conclusive form of 勝つ (katsu, “to win”), and it is possibly related to 片 (kata, “one of a pair”).

sources.quote: Its Heian Kyoto accent pattern LF implies this is the same as 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “conclusive form”) of the verb 勝(か)つ (katsu, “to win”), which has low tone L-. Note the existence of Classical Japanese かつ (katsu, “to be bearable”), homophone of its classical potential form which might have the sense "capable of opposing". Possibly related to 片(かた) (kata, “one of a pair”).

headline: Yosomi is 余所 (yoso, “elsewhere; others”) plus 見 (mi, “looking”).

sources.quote: 余所(よそ) (yoso, “elsewhere; others”) + 見(み) (mi, “looking”)

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Irui is 衣 (i, “clothing; clothes”) plus 類 (rui, “kind; category; group”).

sources.quote: 衣 (i, “clothing; clothes”) + 類 (rui, “kind; category; group”): literally, “[belonging to] the 'clothes' group [of items]”.

headline: Dōkō is uncertain: first attested in 1929, it may be a borrowing from written Chinese, or a coinage from 動 (dō, “moving, movement”) plus 向 (kō, “facing, direction”).

sources.quote: Uncertain. First attested in Japanese in 1929. Might be a borrowing from written Chinese 動向, or possibly a coinage within Japanese of Middle Chinese-derived elements as a compound of 動 (dō, “moving, movement”) + 向 (kō, “facing, direction”).

headline: Hōmuru is often taken as from Old Japanese 葬る (haburu), though the epenthesis of う is uncertain.

sources.quote: Often taken as from Old Japanese 葬る (haburu). But the epenthesis of う is uncertain. Another form of it is 葬(ほうぶ)る (hōburu). Another theory derive it from 火(ほ) (ho) and 埋(う)むる (umuru), 連体形(れんたいけい) (rentaikei) of 埋(う)む (umu) (modern 埋(う)める (umeru), but is phonologically and morphologically problematic.

headline: Gakushi is from Middle Chinese 學士.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 學士 (hæwk dzri^X).

headline: In mosaku, 模 is a daiyōji replacing 摸.

sources.quote: 模 is a daiyōji replacing 摸.

headline: Tamari is the continuative stem of the verb 溜まる (tamaru, “to gather, to accumulate”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 溜(た)まる (tamaru, “to gather, to accumulate”).

headline: Ōgon is from Middle Chinese 黃金 (MC hwang kim, “yellow + metal”).

sources.quote: /wau komʉ/ → /wauɡomʉ/ → /wauɡon/ → /wɔːɡoɴ/ → /oːɡoɴ/
From Middle Chinese 黃金 (MC hwang kim, “yellow + metal”).
Compare modern Cantonese wong⁴ gam¹.

headline: ダウン is from English down.

sources.quote: From English down.

headline: Uwamawaru is the bound form 上 (uwa-) of 上 (ue, “up; top”) plus 回る (mawaru, “to go around; to prevail”).

sources.quote: Compound of 上(うわ) (uwa-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 上(うえ) (ue, “up; top”)) + 回(まわ)る (mawaru, “to go around; to prevail”).

headline: フォーム covers “form” and “foam”, and the source takes both from English.

sources.quote: From English form.
From English foam.

headline: Sentō is from Middle Chinese 戰鬪, and the source compares Mandarin 戰鬥 (zhàndòu).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 戰鬪 (*jiɛ̀n *təuᴴ). Compare Mandarin 戰鬥 /战斗 (zhàndòu), Korean 전투 (jeontu), Vietnamese chiến đấu.

headline: Kiza is short for 気障り (kizawari, “disagreeable”).

sources.quote: Short for 気(き)障(ざわ)り (kizawari, “disagreeable”).

headline: ビールス is a learned borrowing from Latin virus.

sources.quote: Learned borrowing from Latin vīrus.

headline: モニター is from English monitor.

sources.quote: From English monitor.

headline: Muimi is 無 (mu-, “without”) plus 意味 (imi, “meaning”).

sources.quote: 無 (mu-, “without”) + 意味 (imi, “meaning”)

headline: Zeimusho is, by surface analysis, 税務 (zeimu) plus 署 (-sho).

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 税務(ぜいむ) (zeimu) + 署(しょ) (-sho).

headline: Chō, “butterfly”, is from Middle Chinese 蝶 (MC thep|dep) and passed through tepu, tefu, tewu and teu.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 蝶 (MC thep|dep).
Phonological development: tepu → tefu → tewu → teu → tjoː [tɕoː]

headline: Akaji is 赤 (aka, “red”) plus 字 (ji, “characters”), and its “deficit” sense, attested since the Taishō period, comes from marking negative sums in red ink.

sources.quote: From 赤(あか) (aka, “red”) + 字(じ) (ji, “characters”). The “deficit” sense, attested since the Taishō period, relates to the tradition of indicating negative sums in a ledger with red ink. Compare English in the red.

headline: Sanbutsu is from the Middle Chinese compound 產物, literally “produce + thing”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 產物 /产物 (srɛn^X mjut, literally “produce + thing”). Compare modern Min Nan reading sán-bu̍t, Cantonese caan² mat⁶.

headline: Sū, “number”, is from Middle Chinese 數.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 數 (MC srjuX|srjuH).

headline: タレント is a wasei eigo (pseudo-anglicism) derived from English talent.

sources.quote: Wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism), derived from talent. Compare Korean 탤런트 (taelleonteu).

headline: Yurumeru is 緩 (yuru, “loose”) plus める (-meru, “-ify”).

sources.quote: From 緩(ゆる) (yuru, “loose”) + める (-meru, “-ify”).

headline: Ōkata is the classical stem 大 (ofo) plus 方 (kata, “direction, way, side”).

sources.quote: From 大(おほ) (ofo, stem of classical adjective 大(おほ)き (ofoki), modern 大(おお)きい (ōkii, “big”)) + 方(かた) (kata, “direction, way, side”).

headline: Kyūshoku is ultimately from Middle Chinese 給食, literally “to give, to supply + food, meal”, sourced from the Records of the Grand Historian.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 給食 (MC kip zyik, literally “to give, to supply + food, meal”). Sourced from the Chinese work 史記 /史记 (Shǐjì, “Records of the Grand Historian”) completed in 91 BCE.

headline: Juku is originally from Middle Chinese 塾 (MC dzyuwk).

sources.quote: Originally from Middle Chinese 塾 (MC dzyuwk).

headline: In ishō, 装 is a daiyōji replacing 裳.

sources.quote: 装 is a daiyōji replacing 裳.

headline: Nadakai is 名 (na, “name”) plus 高い (takai, “high, lofty”), with takai voiced to dakai by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 名(な) (na, “name”) + 高(たか)い (takai, “high, lofty”).
The takai changes to dakai as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
